ns2-unit-digit-7pow95-minus-3pow58.shortcut: Only the exponents mod 4 matter: 95 → 3 and 58 → 2, so compare 7³ = 343 with 3² = 9. 343 − 9 = 334 ends in 4, and since 7⁹⁵ is far larger than 3⁵⁸ the true difference ends in 4 too.
ns2-unit-digit-7pow95-minus-3pow58.trap: 6 — subtracting the unit digits the wrong way round (9 − 3 = 6) instead of borrowing to get 13 − 9 = 4.

ns2-remainder-2pow51-by-7.shortcut: Powers of 2 leave 2, 4, 1 on division by 7, repeating every 3. The digits of 51 sum to 6, so 51 is a multiple of 3 and 2⁵¹ lands on the last value of the cycle, 1.
ns2-remainder-2pow51-by-7.trap: 2 — reading 51 mod 3 = 0 as the first position of the cycle 2, 4, 1; a zero remainder means the last position.

ns2-largest-four-digit-divisible-88.shortcut: Test the options from the top with 88 = 8 × 11: 9988 fails 8 (988 ÷ 8 is not whole), 9968 fails 11 (9 − 9 + 6 − 8 = −2) and 9954 fails 8, while 9944 passes both (944 = 8 × 118, alternating sum 0).
ns2-largest-four-digit-divisible-88.trap: 9988 — it passes the test for 11 and its last two digits are divisible by 4, so checking 4 in place of 8 accepts it; 988 ÷ 8 = 123.5, so it is a multiple of 44 but not of 88.

ns2-hcf-of-decimals.shortcut: Try the options from the largest: 1.75 does not divide 5.6 (3.2 times) and 0.7 does not divide 1.75 (2.5 times), but 0.35 goes into 1.75, 5.6 and 7 exactly 5, 16 and 20 times.
ns2-hcf-of-decimals.trap: 0.07 — writing 1.75, 5.6 and 7 as 175, 56 and 7 without padding to two decimals, which gives HCF 7 and then 0.07 after shifting two places.

ns2-lcm-of-five-numbers.shortcut: Drop 22 and 54, since they divide 198 and 108. Then test options against 108 = 4 × 27: 1980 is not a multiple of 27 and 2970 is not a multiple of 4, while 5940 = 108 × 55 = 135 × 44 = 198 × 30.
ns2-lcm-of-five-numbers.trap: 2970 — taking the factor 2 only once (2 × 3³ × 5 × 11) and missing the 2² in 108 = 2² × 3³.

ns2-trailing-zeros-125-factorial.shortcut: Zeros in n! = (n − sum of n's digits in base 5) ÷ 4. 125 is 1000 in base 5, digit sum 1, so (125 − 1) ÷ 4 = 31.
ns2-trailing-zeros-125-factorial.trap: 25 — stopping at ⌊125/5⌋ and forgetting the extra five in each multiple of 25 (five more) and the third five in 125 (one more).

ns2-remainder-one-divisible-thirteen.shortcut: Each answer must be 2520k + 1. 3361 fails at once (3360 has digit sum 12, so 9 does not divide it). Divide the rest by 13 from the smallest: 10081 leaves 6, and 17641 = 13 × 1357.
ns2-remainder-one-divisible-thirteen.trap: 3361 — 3360 is divisible by 6, 7, 8 and 10, so it survives a check that skips 9; it also leaves 7 on division by 13.

ns2-remainder-342-then-19.shortcut: Take the simplest such number, 47 itself (k = 0): 47 ÷ 19 leaves 9. Because 19 × 18 = 342, every other number of the form 342k + 47 leaves the same 9.
ns2-remainder-342-then-19.trap: Cannot be determined — assuming the unknown quotient k hides the answer, without checking that 19 divides 342 exactly.

ns2-prime-factors-count.shortcut: Every power of 6 holds two primes, so count 6's exponent twice: 2 × 10 + 17 + 27 = 64.
ns2-prime-factors-count.trap: 54 — adding the exponents 10 + 17 + 27 as they stand, leaving the composite base 6 unsplit.

ns2-greatest-number-same-remainder.shortcut: Two differences are enough: HCF(70, 105) = 35. Trying the largest option first also settles it — 70 leaves 62 from both 62 and 132 but 27 from 237, while 35 leaves 27 every time.
ns2-greatest-number-same-remainder.trap: 70 — the first difference, 132 − 62; it gives both of those the remainder 62 but leaves 27 from 237.

ns2-unit-digit-three-factors.shortcut: Pair 3⁶⁵ with 7⁶⁵ to make 21⁶⁵, which ends in 1. What remains is 6⁵⁹ × 7⁶, and 6 × 9 = 54 ends in 4.
ns2-unit-digit-three-factors.trap: 8 — the unit digit of 3 × 6 = 18, as if 7⁷¹ ended in 1; 71 mod 4 = 3, so it ends in 3 and 8 × 3 = 24 gives 4.

ns2-even-factors-1440.shortcut: With 2⁵ in the factorisation, a factor's power of 2 can be 0 to 5, and five of those six choices make it even: 5/6 of the 36 factors = 30.
ns2-even-factors-1440.trap: 36 — the total number of factors of 1440, forgetting to remove the 6 odd ones (the factors of 45).

ns2-least-added-1056-23.shortcut: Jump to a round multiple: 23 × 50 = 1150, less 23 × 4 = 92, is 1058 — just 2 above 1056.
ns2-least-added-1056-23.trap: 21 — the remainder of 1056 ÷ 23, which is what must be subtracted (1035 = 23 × 45), not added.

ns2-largest-of-four-powers.shortcut: 4³⁰ is 2⁶⁰ in disguise, so those two tie and neither can be the single answer. Of the rest, 3⁴⁰ = 9²⁰ beats 5²⁰ at the same exponent.
ns2-largest-of-four-powers.trap: 2⁶⁰ — chosen for its large exponent; written with exponent 20 it is 8²⁰, smaller than 3⁴⁰ = 9²⁰.

ns2-surd-expression-value.shortcut: Estimate: x = 2 + √3 ≈ 3.732, so x² ≈ 13.93 and x³ ≈ 51.98. Then 51.98 − 27.86 − 26.12 + 5 ≈ 3.00, and every option is a whole number.
ns2-surd-expression-value.trap: 5 — assuming x² − 4x + 1 = 0 wipes out every x term and leaves the constant; (x² − 4x + 1)(x + 2) = x³ − 2x² − 7x + 2, which uses up 2 of the 5.

ns2-factorial-sum-remainder-24.shortcut: Stop at 3!: every term from 4! = 24 on is a multiple of 24. The sum is odd (1 plus even terms), which rules out 6 at a glance, and 1 + 2 + 6 = 9.
ns2-factorial-sum-remainder-24.trap: 15 — it is 24 − 9, the amount needed to reach the next multiple of 24, confused with the remainder itself.

ns2-hcf-lcm-other-number.shortcut: The other number must divide the LCM 693 = 3² × 7 × 11. 66 and 88 are even and 121 needs 11², so only 99 fits.
ns2-hcf-lcm-other-number.trap: 66 — like every option it shares HCF 11 with 77, so a check of the HCF alone passes it; its LCM with 77 is 462, not 693.

ns2-product-4107-hcf-37.shortcut: 4107 is odd, so neither number is even — 74 and 148 are out. Of 37 and 111 the larger is 111, and 37 × 111 = 4107 confirms it.
ns2-product-4107-hcf-37.trap: 37 — the HCF itself, which here is the smaller of the two numbers; the question asks for the larger.

ns2-digits-in-2pow40.trap: 12 — the integer part of 12.04 taken as the digit count, missing the +1 for the leading digit.

ns2-remainder-17pow200-by-18.shortcut: 17² = 289 = 16 × 18 + 1, so 17² leaves 1, and 17²⁰⁰ = (17²)¹⁰⁰ leaves 1 as well.
ns2-remainder-17pow200-by-18.trap: 17 — assuming 17ⁿ always leaves 17; that holds only for odd powers, and 200 is even.

ns2-total-factors-4200.shortcut: Write 4200 = 7 × 600. 600 = 2³ × 3 × 5² has 4 × 2 × 3 = 24 factors, and the coprime 7 doubles the count to 48.
ns2-total-factors-4200.trap: 36 — the count for 2² × 3 × 5² × 7 = 2100, from dropping one factor of 2 in the factorisation.

ns2-sum-of-factors-36.shortcut: A perfect square has an odd sum of factors, which rules out 78 and 96. 1 + 36 + 2 + 18 is already 57, past 55, leaving 91.
ns2-sum-of-factors-36.trap: 55 — the sum of the proper factors only, leaving out 36 itself (91 − 36 = 55).

ns2-greatest-four-digit-lcm.shortcut: Every option ends in 00 with its last three digits divisible by 8, so only the factor 3 in the LCM 600 decides. Digit sums 9, 11, 15, 17 leave 9000 and 9600, and the larger wins.
ns2-greatest-four-digit-lcm.trap: 9800 — the largest option and divisible by 25 and 40, but its digit sum 17 fails 3, so it is not a multiple of 15 or 75.

ns2-missing-digit-divisible-3.shortcut: Cast out threes: 5 + 1, 3 and 2 + 4 vanish, leaving 7, which is 1 more than a multiple of 3. The digit must add 2 more, and 2 is the smallest that does.
ns2-missing-digit-divisible-3.trap: 0 — picked on reflex as the smallest digit; it leaves the digit sum at 22, not a multiple of 3.

ns2-primes-below-fifty.shortcut: Beyond 2 and 3 every prime is 6k ± 1. Below 50 there are 16 such numbers; striking 25, 35 and 49 leaves 13, and adding 2 and 3 gives 15.
ns2-primes-below-fifty.trap: 14 — scanning only the odd numbers and missing 2, the one even prime.

ns2-least-subtracted-9999-45.shortcut: The result must end in 0 or 5 and have a digit sum divisible by 9: 9999 − 9 = 9990 (digit sum 27) does both.
ns2-least-subtracted-9999-45.trap: 36 — it is 45 − 9, the amount to add (9999 + 36 = 10035 = 45 × 223), confused with the amount to subtract.

ns2-sum-odd-numbers-100-200.shortcut: The first n odd numbers sum to n². Odd numbers up to 199 are the first 100 (sum 10,000) and up to 99 the first 50 (sum 2,500), so 10,000 − 2,500 = 7500.
ns2-sum-odd-numbers-100-200.trap: Counting the terms as (199 − 101) ÷ 2 = 49, without the + 1 for the first term, gives 49 × 150 = 7350, and the nearest option to that is 7250; the run 101, 103, …, 199 has 50 terms, so the sum is 50 × 150 = 7500.

ns2-telescoping-series.shortcut: The first term alone is 1/2 and the endless series sums to 1, so the answer lies strictly between 1/2 and 1 — only 9/10 does.
ns2-telescoping-series.trap: 1/10 — keeping the leftover 1/10 from the cancellation and forgetting the leading 1, so 1 − 1/10 becomes just 1/10.

ns2-difference-of-consecutive-odd-square.shortcut: Test the smallest pair: 3² − 1² = 8, and of the options only 8 divides 8.
ns2-difference-of-consecutive-odd-square.trap: 6 — testing only 5 and 7 gives 49 − 25 = 24, which 6 divides; the pair 3 and 5 gives 16, which it does not.

ns2-remainder-sum-of-powers.shortcut: Fermat's little theorem gives 17⁶ ≡ 1 (mod 7) with no work, since 7 is prime and does not divide 17; 6 ≡ −1 makes 6¹⁷ ≡ −1, and the two cancel to 0.
ns2-remainder-sum-of-powers.trap: 6 — the remainder of 6¹⁷ alone, as if 17⁶ added nothing; 17⁶ leaves 1, and 6 + 1 = 7 leaves 0.

ns2-count-multiples-between.shortcut: LCM 60: ⌊600/60⌋ − ⌊200/60⌋ = 10 − 3 = 7 counts 600 itself, and 'between' excludes it, leaving 6.
ns2-count-multiples-between.trap: 7 — counting 600 as one of the numbers; 'between 200 and 600' shuts out the endpoint.

ns2-6n-squared-plus-6n.shortcut: n = 1 gives 12, so any number that always divides the expression must divide 12 — 18 and 24 are out. 12 is the fuller guarantee, since n(n + 1) is always even.
ns2-6n-squared-plus-6n.trap: 24 — n = 3 and n = 4 give 72 and 120, both multiples of 24, but n = 1 gives 12 and n = 2 gives 36, neither of which 24 divides.

ns2-crt-two-conditions.shortcut: Both remainders fall 2 short of the divisor (5 − 3 = 7 − 5 = 2), so N + 2 is a multiple of 35 and the smallest N is 35 − 2 = 33.
ns2-crt-two-conditions.trap: 23 — the first option that leaves 3 on division by 5; 23 ÷ 7 leaves 2, not 5.

ns2-unit-digit-4pow54.shortcut: 4⁵⁴ = 16²⁷, and every power of 16 ends in 6.
ns2-unit-digit-4pow54.trap: 4 — assuming the power keeps the base's unit digit, which is true for 4 only at odd exponents.

ns2-power-equation.trap: 125 — from taking 3125 as 5⁶ (5⁶ is 15,625), which makes x − 3 = 3.

ns2-sum-first-20-even.shortcut: The 20 evens run 2 to 40 with average 21, so the sum is 20 × 21 = 420.
ns2-sum-first-20-even.trap: 400 — using n² = 20², the formula for the first n odd numbers.

ns2-least-added-4321-19.shortcut: Peel off round multiples of 19: 4321 − 3800 = 521, 521 − 380 = 141, 141 − 133 = 8, so 4321 leaves 8 and needs 19 − 8 = 11 more.
ns2-least-added-4321-19.trap: 8 — the remainder of 4321 ÷ 19, which is the amount to subtract (4313 = 19 × 227), not to add.

ns2-three-digit-divisible-by-9-and-11.shortcut: Test from the top: 999 fails 11 (alternating sum 9), while 990 has digit sum 18 and alternating sum 0, so it passes both tests.
ns2-three-digit-divisible-by-9-and-11.trap: 999 — the largest three-digit number and a multiple of 9, but 999 ÷ 11 leaves 9.

ns2-remainder-power-of-three-mod-five.shortcut: A remainder on division by 5 follows from the unit digit. 3²¹ ends in 3 (21 leaves 1 on division by 4), and a number ending in 3 leaves 3.
ns2-remainder-power-of-three-mod-five.trap: 1 — stopping at 3²⁰ = (3⁴)⁵, which leaves 1, and forgetting the one extra factor of 3.

ns2-number-of-zeros-in-product.shortcut: Count fives term by term: each of the ten terms holds one, and 50 and 100 each hold a second, so 10 + 2 = 12; twos are plentiful.
ns2-number-of-zeros-in-product.trap: 11 — counting the zeros printed in the terms (one each in 10 to 90, two in 100); the extra five in 50 pairs with a spare 2 to make a twelfth.

tw2-a10-b15-together.shortcut: For two workers, time together = product ÷ sum: 10 × 15 ÷ 25 = 6 days.
tw2-a10-b15-together.trap: 5 days — half of A's 10 days, as if B were as fast as A; B is slower, so the pair need longer than 5.

tw2-a6-b10-together.trap: 4 days — 30 ÷ 8 rounded to a whole day out of habit, since most answers in the chapter are integers; the exact 3.75 days is on offer.

tw2-together-8-a-12-b-alone.shortcut: For the missing partner, time = product ÷ difference: 8 × 12 ÷ (12 − 8) = 96 ÷ 4 = 24 days.
tw2-together-8-a-12-b-alone.trap: 20 days — adding the two times (8 + 12); rates subtract, but times do not.

tw2-twice-efficient-12.shortcut: B supplies 1 of the pair's 3 shares of output, so alone B needs 3 × 12 = 36 days (and A needs 1.5 × 12 = 18).
tw2-twice-efficient-12.trap: 18 days — A's time alone; A is the faster worker, while the question asks about B.

tw2-three-times-good-60-less.shortcut: Times are in the ratio 1 : 3, so the 60-day gap is 2 parts: A 30, B 90. Together = 30 × 90 ÷ 120 = 22.5 days.
tw2-three-times-good-60-less.trap: 30 days — A's time alone, stopping before combining the two rates.

tw2-25-percent-more-efficient.shortcut: Efficiency 5 : 4 means time 4 : 5, so the 10-day gap is one part and A takes 4 × 10 = 40 days.
tw2-25-percent-more-efficient.trap: 50 — B's time, the first number the equation 0.2t = 10 produces; A takes 0.8 × 50.

tw2-abc-together-4-c-alone.shortcut: Back-substitute: with C = 9, 1/12 + 1/18 + 1/9 = 3/36 + 2/36 + 4/36 = 9/36 = 1/4, exactly the trio's rate.
tw2-abc-together-4-c-alone.trap: 6 days — subtracting only A's rate (1/4 − 1/12 = 1/6) and forgetting to take B's off as well.

tw2-pairs-abc.shortcut: Take 60 units: the pairs do 5, 4 and 3 a day, which counts each person twice, so the trio does 12 ÷ 2 = 6 a day and needs 60 ÷ 6 = 10 days.
tw2-pairs-abc.trap: 12 days — the fastest pair's time, as if adding C changed nothing; a third worker must make the job quicker than any pair.

tw2-a-alone-from-pairs.shortcut: Take 30 units: the trio does 3 a day and B + C does 2, so A does 1 a day — 30 days. The A + B figure is never needed.
tw2-a-alone-from-pairs.trap: 60 days — subtracting the wrong pair (1/10 − 1/12 = 1/60), which gives C's time, not A's.

tw2-a-works-5-then-b-finishes.shortcut: A would have needed 10 more days for the rest; B needed 12, so B is 1.2 times as slow: 1.2 × 15 = 18 days.
tw2-a-works-5-then-b-finishes.trap: 24 days — doubling B's 12 days as if A had done half the job; A did only a third.

tw2-together-4-days-b-finishes.shortcut: A's 4 days cover 4/12 = 1/3 of the job, so B does 2/3 — 10 of his 15 days. He has already worked 4, leaving 6.
tw2-together-4-days-b-finishes.trap: 5 days — taking the work left as the third that A did (4/12) rather than the 2/5 still undone; 1/3 × 15 = 5.

tw2-together-20-b-leaves.shortcut: The pair would have finished the last third in 10 days; A alone took 20, so A works at half the pair's rate and needs 2 × 30 = 60 days.
tw2-together-20-b-leaves.trap: 50 days — adding A's extra 20 days to the pair's 30, as if the solo stint only stretched the schedule; those 20 days cover just the last third.

tw2-a-leaves-five-days-before.shortcut: Pretend A stays to the end: he would add 5/20 = 1/4 of a job, so the pair (12 days a job, 20 × 30 ÷ 50) would finish 1¼ jobs in the time: 1.25 × 12 = 15 days.
tw2-a-leaves-five-days-before.trap: 12 days — the time if both worked throughout, ignoring that A leaves early.

tw2-alternate-days-20-30.shortcut: Two alternate days equal one joint day. The pair together need 20 × 30 ÷ 50 = 12 days, a whole number, so alternation takes exactly 24.
tw2-alternate-days-20-30.trap: 25 days — adding a day for A to finish off, without noticing that the 12 two-day cycles land exactly on the whole job.

tw2-alternate-pipes.shortcut: In 12 units, every A-then-B pair of hours adds 5, so after 4 hours 2 units remain and the turn is A's; 2 of A's 3 units an hour take 40 minutes.
tw2-alternate-pipes.trap: 5 h — giving the fifth hour to B, whose 2 units an hour would fill the last 2 units in exactly an hour; A started, so the fifth hour is A's.

tw2-pipes-two-in-one-out.shortcut: Call the tank 60 units: A adds 5 and B 4 an hour, C removes 3, so the net is 6 an hour and the tank fills in 10 hours.
tw2-pipes-two-in-one-out.trap: 12 h — A's time alone, on the idea that B's inflow roughly cancels C's outflow; B adds 4 units an hour but C removes only 3, so the tank fills sooner.

tw2-leak-empties-full.shortcut: Filler against leak: time = product ÷ difference = 6 × 12 ÷ (12 − 6) = 12 hours.
tw2-leak-empties-full.trap: 18 h — adding the two times (6 + 12); the leak removes half the tap's rate, which doubles 6 hours to 12.

tw2-leak-adds-an-hour.shortcut: Leak time = product ÷ difference of the two filling times: 4 × 5 ÷ (5 − 4) = 20 hours.
tw2-leak-adds-an-hour.trap: 10 h — half of 4 × 5, from dividing by 2 as if the delay were two hours; the delay is one hour, so the product itself is the answer.

tw2-cistern-nine-to-ten.shortcut: Leak time = product ÷ difference of the two filling times: 9 × 10 ÷ (10 − 9) = 90 hours.
tw2-cistern-nine-to-ten.trap: 45 h — half of 9 × 10, from dividing by 2 as if the delay were two hours; with a one-hour gap, product ÷ difference = 90 ÷ 1.

tw2-close-one-pipe.shortcut: Had the first pipe run all 18 minutes, 18/20 + 18/30 = 1.5 tanks would flow; the extra half tank is 10 minutes of the first pipe, so it shut after 18 − 10 = 8 minutes.
tw2-close-one-pipe.trap: 12 min — giving the first pipe the 3/5 that the second pipe supplies (3/5 × 20 = 12) instead of the remaining 2/5.

tw2-both-open-4-min-then-one.shortcut: The second pipe runs throughout and must supply 1 − 4/10 = 3/5 of the tank, which is 9 of its 15 minutes; 9 − 4 = 5 more.
tw2-both-open-4-min-then-one.trap: 4 min — tempting because it echoes the 4 minutes already run; the joint run filled 2/3, and the last third at 1/15 a minute takes 5.

tw2-waste-pipe-capacity.shortcut: Call the cistern 120 units: the taps give 7 a minute and the net is 2, so the waste pipe removes 5 units = 3 gallons a minute, and 120 units = 120 × 3/5 = 72 gallons.
tw2-waste-pipe-capacity.trap: Multiplying the waste pipe's 3 gallons a minute by the 60-minute fill gives 180 gallons — what the pipe drains while the cistern fills, not what it holds; the pipe alone would empty the cistern in 24 minutes, so the capacity is 24 × 3 gallons.

tw2-men-and-women-equivalence.shortcut: Count in men: 4 women = 2 men, so the team is 6 men, twice the 3 who need 20 days — 10 days.
tw2-men-and-women-equivalence.trap: 15 days — counting all 8 workers as women (120 woman-days ÷ 8); the 4 men are worth 8 women.

tw2-women-and-children.shortcut: 5 women are half a 7-day crew, so alone they need 14 days — the same as the 10 children. Two 14-day teams together take 7 days.
tw2-women-and-children.trap: 3.5 days — halving 7 on the reflex that two groups halve the time; that holds only if each group alone takes 7 days, and here each takes 14.

tw2-men-days-to-more-men.shortcut: Time falls to 6/8 = 3/4, so the crew rises by 4/3: 12 × 4/3 = 16 men.
tw2-men-days-to-more-men.trap: 14 — adding the 2 days saved to the 12 men, a direct adjustment where an inverse one is needed.

tw2-more-men-join.shortcut: The last 12 days' work for 12 men takes 16 men 12 × 12/16 = 9 days, so the total is 8 + 9 = 17.
tw2-more-men-join.trap: 16 days — cutting the remaining 12 days by a third because the crew grew by a third; a third more men cuts time by a quarter, to 9 days.

tw2-men-leave.shortcut: What is left is 12 days' work for 24 men; 16 men need 12 × 24/16 = 18 days.
tw2-men-leave.trap: 16 days — adding a third to the remaining 12 days because a third of the men left; two thirds of the crew need 3/2 of the time, 18 days.

tw2-contractor-more-men.shortcut: 100 men do a third of the job in 15 days; doing the last third in 10 days needs 100 × 15/10 = 150 men, so 50 more.
tw2-contractor-more-men.trap: 100 — doubling the crew on the feeling that the last third must go twice as fast; it must go 1.5 times as fast (a third in 10 days, not 15).

tw2-hectares-reaped.shortcut: 80 hectares per 192 man-days is 5 hectares per 12 man-days; 36 × 30 = 1,080 man-days is 90 such blocks, so 450 hectares.
tw2-hectares-reaped.trap: 360 — scaling by the men alone (80 × 36/8) and forgetting the move from 24 to 30 days.

tw2-wall-length.shortcut: Man-days go from 120 to 105, a ratio of 7/8, so the wall is 56 × 7/8 = 49 m.
tw2-wall-length.trap: 56 m — assuming 35 men for half the days cancels out; 35 is 1.75 times 20, not twice, so output falls to 7/8 of 56.

tw2-hours-per-day.trap: 15 days — the nearest option to 15.6, which is what ignoring the change from 5-hour to 6-hour days gives (12 × 39 ÷ 30).

tw2-men-women-hours.trap: 20 — counting the 21 women as 21 men (21 × 15/21 × 8/6 = 20); they are worth only 14 men.

tw2-half-and-third.shortcut: In 5 days together they finish 1/2 + 1/3 = 5/6 of the job, so the whole takes 5 × 6/5 = 6 days.
tw2-half-and-third.trap: 5 days — treating a half plus a third as the whole job; 1/2 + 1/3 = 5/6 leaves a sixth undone.

tw2-four-fifths-in-20.shortcut: Work left : work done = 1 : 4, so the time left is 20 ÷ 4 = 5 days; the whole job is 25 days, which checks.
tw2-four-fifths-in-20.trap: 4 days — dividing 20 by 5 (the denominator) instead of by 4, the number of fifths already done.

tw2-payment-share-c.shortcut: In the 3 days A does 3/6 = 1/2 and B does 3/8, so C's part is 1 − 1/2 − 3/8 = 1/8, and 600 ÷ 8 = ₹75.
tw2-payment-share-c.trap: Paying C his one-day fraction — 1/24 of ₹600 = ₹25 — forgets that he works all 3 days; his part of the job is 3 × 1/24 = 1/8, so he earns an eighth of the ₹600.

tw2-abc-help-c-alone.shortcut: In the 4 days A does 4/8 = 1/2 and B 4/12 = 1/3, leaving C 1/6 of the job in 4 days — so C alone needs 24.
tw2-abc-help-c-alone.trap: 20 days — adding A's and B's times (8 + 12); times never add, and C's rate is 1/4 − 1/8 − 1/12 = 1/24.

tw2-tank-tap-and-leak-capacity.shortcut: The tap's filling time is product ÷ difference of the two emptying times: 8 × 12 ÷ 4 = 24 hours, and 24 × 360 L = 8,640 L.
tw2-tank-tap-and-leak-capacity.trap: 4,320 L — multiplying the tap's 360 L an hour by the 12-hour emptying time instead of the tap's own 24-hour filling time.

tw2-b-alone-after-a-quits.shortcut: B's rate is half of (A + B) + (B + C) − (A + C). In 60 units that is (6 + 4 − 5) ÷ 2 = 2.5 a day, so 60 ÷ 2.5 = 24 days.
tw2-b-alone-after-a-quits.trap: 40 days — subtracting the wrong pair (1/8 − 1/10 = 1/40), which gives C's time, not B's.

ns-remainder-power-of-seven.shortcut: The remainder on 5 can be read off the unit digit: 7¹⁰⁰ ends in 1 because 100 is a multiple of 4, so it leaves 1.
ns-remainder-power-of-seven.trap: 2 — treating 100 mod 4 = 0 as the first position of the cycle 2, 4, 3, 1; a zero remainder means the last position.

ns-unit-digit-product.shortcut: Pair them: 3²³ × 7²³ = 21²³ ends in 1, leaving 3²⁴ = 81⁶, which also ends in 1.
ns-unit-digit-product.trap: 9 — reading 3⁴⁷ as ending in 3 (as if 47 left 1 on division by 4) and multiplying by the 3 from 7²³.

ns-hcf-lcm-product.shortcut: The other number must be a multiple of 12 that divides 360: 48 and 90 fail at once, and 120 shares 24 with 72, leaving 60.
ns-hcf-lcm-product.trap: 120 — a multiple of 12 whose LCM with 72 is indeed 360, but HCF(72, 120) = 24, not 12.

ns-divisible-by-nine-digit.shortcut: Cast out nines: 4 + 5 vanishes, leaving 3, so x must bring the total to a multiple of 9: x = 6.
ns-divisible-by-nine-digit.trap: 3 — it makes the digit sum 15, which passes the test for 3 but not for 9.

ns-count-of-divisors.shortcut: √360 ≈ 19, and the divisors below it — 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10, 12, 15, 18 — number 12. Each pairs with one above, so 24.
ns-count-of-divisors.trap: 18 — the count for 2² × 3² × 5 = 180, from dropping one factor of 2 when factorising 360.

ns-trailing-zeros-factorial.shortcut: Zeros in n! = (n − sum of n's digits in base 5) ÷ 4. 100 is 400 in base 5, digit sum 4, so (100 − 4) ÷ 4 = 24.
ns-trailing-zeros-factorial.trap: 20 — stopping at ⌊100/5⌋ and missing the extra five in each of 25, 50, 75 and 100.

ns-consecutive-odd-sum.shortcut: Back-substitute from the options: 23 as the largest gives 19, 21, 23, which sum to 63.
ns-consecutive-odd-sum.trap: 21 — the middle number, 63 ÷ 3, given as the answer when the question asks for the largest.

pc-successive-up-down.shortcut: Write it as (1 + 0.2)(1 − 0.2) = 1 − 0.2² = 0.96: a difference of squares, so an equal rise and fall always ends below the start.
pc-successive-up-down.trap: No change — assuming +20% and −20% cancel; the 20% cut is taken from the larger 120, so it removes 24.

pc-population-growth.shortcut: Add 10% twice, the second 10% also on the first year's gain: 5,000 + 5,000 + 500 = 10,500 added, giving 60,500.
pc-population-growth.trap: 60,000 — adding 20% as simple growth; the second year's 10% is on 55,000, not 50,000.

pc-failing-marks.trap: 540 — the nearest option to 240 ÷ 0.45 ≈ 533, which is what forgetting to add the 30 missing marks gives.

pc-more-than-less-than.shortcut: 25% more is 1/4 more; the reverse is 1/(4 + 1) = 1/5 less, i.e. 20%.
pc-more-than-less-than.trap: 25% — assuming the reverse change is the same percentage; the gap of 25 is measured against A's 125, not B's 100.

pc-share-percentage-points.shortcut: Divide new by old: 36 ÷ 30 = 1.2, a 20% rise.
pc-share-percentage-points.trap: 6% — the rise in percentage points (36 − 30) read as a percentage change.

pc-consumption-cut.shortcut: Spending fixed means price × consumption is constant: price × 5/4, so consumption × 4/5 — a cut of 1/5 = 20%.
pc-consumption-cut.trap: 25% — matching the price rise; a 25% cut with a 25% rise leaves spending at 1.25 × 0.75 = 93.75% of the old amount.

pl-selling-price-from-profit.shortcut: 10% of 800 is 80 and 5% is 40, so the profit is 120 and the price ₹920.
pl-selling-price-from-profit.trap: ₹880 — adding only 10% (₹80) and dropping the extra 5% (₹40).

pl-markup-then-discount.shortcut: Net change = a + b + ab/100 with b = −10: 40 − 10 − 4 = 26%.
pl-markup-then-discount.trap: 30% — subtracting the 10% discount from the 40% markup; the discount is taken on 140, so it removes 14, not 10.

pl-equal-selling-price.shortcut: The loss-making article cost more (₹1,500 against ₹1,000), so the loss outweighs the gain, ruling out break-even and any profit; the loss is 100 on 2,500 = 4%.
pl-equal-selling-price.trap: No profit, no loss — assuming an equal 20% gain and 20% loss cancel; the percentages are on different cost prices.

pl-false-weight.shortcut: The dealer hands over 9 parts and charges for 10, so the profit is 1/9 of the cost = 11.11%.
pl-false-weight.trap: 10% — dividing the 100 g saved by 1,000 g; profit is measured on the 900 g actually delivered.

pl-sp-of-20-equals-cp-of-25.shortcut: The 5 extra articles' worth is profit earned on 20 articles, so profit = 5/20 = 25%.
pl-sp-of-20-equals-cp-of-25.trap: 20% — dividing the 5 by 25 instead of 20; profit is measured on the cost of the 20 articles sold.

pl-successive-discounts.shortcut: The second 10% comes off 80, not 100, so it removes only 8: 20 + 8 = 28%.
pl-successive-discounts.trap: 30% — adding the two discounts (20 + 10); the second applies to the already reduced price.

rp-divide-in-ratio.shortcut: C's share is 4/9 of the total, just under half: 4/9 of 5,400 = 2,400, and no other option is near 44%.
rp-divide-in-ratio.trap: ₹1,800 — an equal three-way split (5,400 ÷ 3), which is also B's share of 3 parts; C holds 4 parts.

rp-combine-two-ratios.trap: 2 : 3 : 5 — writing the ratios side by side without making B's two values (3 and 4) equal.

rp-partnership-time-weighted.shortcut: Capital ratio 2 : 3 and time ratio 12 : 8 = 3 : 2 cancel exactly, so the profit splits evenly.
rp-partnership-time-weighted.trap: A ₹8,000, B ₹10,000 — the option nearest a split by capital alone (2 : 3 gives ₹7,200 and ₹10,800); B's shorter time cancels his larger stake.

rp-coins-in-a-bag.shortcut: Back-substitute: 60 fifty-paise coins means 40 rupee coins and 80 25-paise coins, worth 40 + 30 + 20 = ₹90.
rp-coins-in-a-bag.trap: 40 — the number of ₹1 coins (2 parts × 20 sets), read from the wrong place in the ratio.

rp-inverse-variation-workers.shortcut: Men rise by 15/12 = 5/4, so days fall by 4/5: 20 × 4/5 = 16.
rp-inverse-variation-workers.trap: 25 — treating it as direct variation (20 × 15/12); more men need fewer days, not more.

rp-fourth-proportional.shortcut: 6 is 1.5 times 4, so the fourth term is 1.5 times 10 = 15.
rp-fourth-proportional.trap: 12 — adding the difference (10 + 2) instead of keeping the ratio; proportion means equal ratios, not equal gaps.

av-teacher-joins.trap: 45 — 15 + 30 × 1, which lifts the 30 students but forgets that the teacher also sits at the new average of 16.

av-replacement.shortcut: Test by difference: (85 − 65) ÷ 8 = 2.5 exactly, while 80 and 90 give 1.875 and 3.125.
av-replacement.trap: 90 kg — adding 25 to 65 (2.5 read as 25, or multiplied by 10 rather than by the 8 people).

av-consecutive-even.shortcut: Five evenly spaced evens sit at −4, −2, 0, +2, +4 around the mean, so the largest is 24 + 4 = 28.
av-consecutive-even.trap: 26 — the answer for five consecutive integers (22 to 26); even numbers are 2 apart, so the top is two steps of 2 above 24.

av-misread-entry.shortcut: 64 and 46 are the same digits swapped, and a swap always errs by 9 × the digit gap = 9 × 2 = 18, so the average rises by 1.8.
av-misread-entry.trap: 44.2 — subtracting 46 from 64 digit by digit without borrowing (22 instead of 18), so the rise becomes 2.2.

av-batsman-innings.shortcut: Check an option: 17 × 43 = 731, and 16 × 40 + 91 = 640 + 91 = 731 — they match, so 43.
av-batsman-innings.trap: 45 — the option nearest 731 ÷ 16 ≈ 45.7, which comes from dividing the new total by the old count of 16 innings instead of 17.

av-first-fifty-naturals.shortcut: Pair 1 with 50, 2 with 49 and so on: all 25 pairs total 51, so every pair averages 25.5.
av-first-fifty-naturals.trap: 25 — taking half of 50 rather than the midpoint of 1 and 50.

ag-father-thrice-son.shortcut: When the father is twice the son, the age gap equals the son's age. The gap is 2s now, so 2s = s + 12 and s = 12.
ag-father-thrice-son.trap: Expanding 2(s + 12) as 2s + 12 — doubling the son's age but not the years added to it — gives s = 0, and a solver who then checks the options by eye can accept 14: father 42, then 54 against 26, which looks like twice but is 2 more than 2 × 26.

ag-ratio-now-and-later.shortcut: Back-substitute: A = 30 makes B = 42, and six years on 36 : 48 = 3 : 4.
ag-ratio-now-and-later.trap: 42 — B's present age (7 × 6), picked when the question asks for A's.

ag-mother-daughter-sum.shortcut: Five years ago the ages summed to 50 − 10 = 40, split 7 : 1 into 35 and 5; the mother is now 35 + 5 = 40.
ag-mother-daughter-sum.trap: 35 — the mother's age five years ago, given without adding the 5 years back.

ag-ten-years-ago-half.shortcut: The sum is 3k + 4k = 7k, and 35 is the only option divisible by 7.
ag-ten-years-ago-half.trap: Taking the ten years off Ram's age but not Shyam's — 2(3k − 10) = 4k — gives k = 10 and ages of 30 and 40, both of which sit among the options; Shyam was ten years younger too, so 2(3k − 10) = 4k − 10, k = 5 and the sum is 35.

ag-product-and-difference.shortcut: With a gap of 2, the mean age m satisfies (m − 1)(m + 1) = m² − 1 = 48, so m = 7 and the sum is 14.
ag-product-and-difference.trap: 16 — the sum of 4 and 12, another factor pair of 48 grabbed without checking that their difference is 8, not 2.

ag-percent-of-past-and-future.shortcut: 125% = 5/4, so present : past = 5 : 4. The one-part gap is 10 years, so the present age is 5 × 10 = 50.
ag-percent-of-past-and-future.trap: 60 — his age 10 years hence, the base of the 83⅓%, given in place of the present age.

cl4-shop-week-highest-day.shortcut: Only days above the 200 average can win: Thursday (220) and Friday (250), and Friday is larger.
cl4-shop-week-highest-day.trap: Thursday — at 220 it is the first figure above 200 in a top-down scan, easy to settle on before reaching Friday's 250.

cl4-shop-week-average.shortcut: Measure from 200: −50, 0, −20, +20, +50, 0 sum to zero, so the average is 200.
cl4-shop-week-average.trap: 180 — the option nearest 1,200 ÷ 7 ≈ 171, which comes from dividing by a full week; the shop opened only six days.

cl4-shop-week-wednesday-share.shortcut: 1% of 1,200 is 12, and 180 ÷ 12 = 15, so the share is 15%.
cl4-shop-week-wednesday-share.trap: 18% — reading 180 out of 1,000, as if the total were a round thousand instead of 1,200.

tc4-marks-highest-total.shortcut: Measure each mark from 75: Amit +2 − 10 + 7 = −1, Bina +10 − 3 − 7 = 0, Chetan −9 + 15 − 1 = +5, Divya +17 − 17 + 1 = +1. Chetan leads.
tc4-marks-highest-total.trap: Divya — she has the top single mark (92 in Maths), but her 58 in Physics holds her total to 226, below Chetan's 230.

tc4-marks-average-maths.shortcut: Measure from 80: −3, +5, −14, +12 sum to zero, so the average is 80.
tc4-marks-average-maths.trap: 76 — the option nearest the average of all twelve marks (905 ÷ 12 ≈ 75.4), from averaging the whole table instead of the Maths column.

sc4-along-with-agreement.shortcut: Three of the four verbs — were, are, have been — are plural. With 'along with the students' set aside the subject is 'the teacher', so the one singular verb, was, wins.
sc4-along-with-agreement.trap: "The teacher along with the students were present." — the verb is pulled into agreeing with the nearer plural noun, students.

sc4-neither-of-the-two.shortcut: Read neither as 'not one': 'not one of the two candidates was selected' — a singular verb with a plural noun after 'of the two'. Only one option has both.
sc4-neither-of-the-two.trap: "Neither of the two candidates were selected." — the verb agrees with the plural candidates beside it instead of the singular subject, neither.

sc4-since-versus-for.shortcut: Since needs a point in time, so every option with 'since five years' is out; three use it, leaving the one with 'for'.
sc4-since-versus-for.trap: "I have been living here since five years." — its tense is right, which makes it look correct, but a stretch of time takes for, not since.

sc4-scarcely-when.shortcut: Only 'no sooner', a comparative, takes than; scarcely and hardly are not comparatives and pair with when.
sc4-scarcely-when.trap: than — borrowed from 'no sooner … than', the pair most candidates learn first.
